results.result: The authors developed an open-source software (I-Spin) for real-time motor unit identification using blind-source separation. The software uses fastICA to optimize separation vectors for each motor unit, projects EMG signals onto these vectors to generate sparse pulse trains, and classifies peaks as discharge times using k-means classification. The software supports multiple electrode types and acquisition systems, provides three forms of visual feedback (raster plot, quadrant, smoothed firing rate), and follows a four-step framework for real-time identification.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C35 collectively describe the software development and its technical implementation. The description is internally consistent and provides sufficient methodological detail. The software is made publicly available (C19), fulfilling the claim of being open-source. The technical approach is based on established methods (C30) and is clearly documented.

results.result: Validation using synthetic EMG signals demonstrated high accuracy of the algorithm. Offline decomposition achieved 100.0±0.0% agreement for intramuscular and 99.2±1.8% for surface EMG. Real-time application of filters from 20% MVC baseline to sinusoidal contractions achieved 96.3±4.6% (surface) and 98.4±2.3% (intramuscular) agreement. Accuracy remained high when applied to 10% MVC (>99.5%) but decreased at 30% MVC (80.3-88.6%) due to recruitment of spatially overlapping motor units.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C58 present simulation validation results with clear quantitative metrics. The simulation methodology is properly cited (C47, C49) and results show expected patterns: high accuracy for matched conditions, maintained accuracy for lower forces, and decreased accuracy for higher forces due to motor unit merging (C58). The explanation for decreased accuracy at 30% MVC is mechanistically sound and supported by the data.

results.result: Experimental validation in tibialis anterior (8 participants, 144 motor units) showed rates of agreement of 95.6±6.8% (10% MVC) and 93.9±5.9% (20% MVC) when test and baseline forces matched. When filters from 20% MVC were applied to 10% MVC signals, agreement decreased to 87.9±16.2% with high precision (99.4±4.3%) but lower sensitivity (88.0±16.2%), indicating missed discharge times. When filters from 10% MVC were applied to 20% MVC, agreement decreased to 83.3±13.5% with both sensitivity (90.7±8.1%) and precision (90.9±12.6%) affected, confirming that motor units recruited between force levels disrupt accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C69 present experimental validation with appropriate sample size and clear metrics. The pattern of results is consistent with simulation findings (C69) and the interpretation is mechanistically sound. High precision but lower sensitivity when applying higher-force filters to lower forces (C65-C66) indicates missed spikes rather than false positives, which is the expected behavior. The bidirectional testing (both up and down in force) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Multi-muscle validation (21 male participants, 5 muscles) showed variable accuracy across muscles. At 20% MVC, tibialis anterior showed highest agreement (93.6±9.2% surface grid, 97.3±5.2% intramuscular), while vastii (VL: 82.1±19.7%; VM: 75.3±18.5%) and gastrocnemii (GL: 88.1±7.8%; GM: 81.0±17.7%) showed lower agreement. At 40% MVC, rates ranged from 75.2±20.6% (VM) to 87.9±8.7% (GM).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75 present systematic multi-muscle validation with clear quantitative results. The between-muscle differences are substantial and consistently show TA > gastrocnemii > vastii in terms of accuracy. The sample sizes vary by muscle but are adequate for the conclusions drawn. The higher accuracy with intramuscular arrays (C73) is consistent with theoretical expectations and prior work.

results.result: Biofeedback accuracy was assessed by comparing real-time to edited firing rates. RMSE was consistently below 2 pps at 20% MVC across all muscles, with lowest values for TA (0.64±0.77 pps surface, 0.44±0.43 pps intramuscular). At 40% MVC, RMSE ranged from 0.6±0.4 pps (GM) to 1.8±1.1 pps (VM). These low RMSE values indicate the biofeedback accurately reflected motor unit firing activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80, C107 present biofeedback validation with appropriate metrics (RMSE). The values are consistently low (<2 pps) and show the expected pattern of better performance with intramuscular arrays. The inference that low RMSE indicates accurate biofeedback (C80, C107) is reasonable given the magnitude of the errors relative to typical firing rates (which appear to be 5-10 pps based on figures).

results.result: Manual editing substantially improved motor unit identification quality. At 20% MVC, automatic decomposition identified 10-25 motor units per muscle, with SIL values of 0.82-0.95. After removing 1-21 motor units per muscle through visual inspection and manual editing, remaining motor units showed improved SIL values (0.89-0.95). A SIL threshold of ~0.9 can be used to automatically filter poor quality motor units, though visual inspection after sessions remains necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 document the manual editing process with clear quantitative outcomes. The improvement in SIL values after editing (C42 vs C40) supports the effectiveness of manual editing. The large number of removed motor units (especially for GL: 21±12 at 20% MVC, C41) highlights the importance of this step. The recommendation for a SIL threshold of 0.9 (C45) is supported by the data, though the caveat about visual inspection (C46) is appropriate given algorithm limitations.

results.result: Computational performance analysis showed the system operates in real-time. For surface electrodes, decomposition time averaged 4.9±3.0 ms with 0.37 ms per motor unit (maximum 13.1 ms for 26 units). Intramuscular recordings required 32.0 ms for 9 units due to higher sampling frequency. Feedback display added 8.6±5.7 ms (raster) or 11.2±7.6 ms (smoothed rates). Total computational time remained below the 125 ms epoch duration, resulting in only the incompressible 125 ms recording delay.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C126 present comprehensive computational performance data. The linear relationship between motor units and computational time (C117) is well-characterized. The explanation for longer intramuscular processing time (C120) is mechanistically sound. The critical finding that total time < epoch duration (C125) validates the real-time capability, with the 125 ms delay (C126) being the minimum possible given the epoch-based processing approach.

results.result: The algorithm's accuracy depends on two key assumptions: (1) uniqueness of motor unit action potential distributions across electrodes, and (2) consistency of motor unit filters across time. When uniqueness is violated, merged motor units cause false positives. Intramuscular arrays show higher accuracy due to lower likelihood of spatial overlap. Filter consistency can be disrupted by muscle geometry changes during contraction, including muscle bulking during shortening and changes in pennation angle, leading to the recommendation for isometric contractions with stable force.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 describe the theoretical basis and limitations of the algorithm. The uniqueness assumption (C81) is well-supported by citations and the consequences of violation (C82) are demonstrated in the experimental data (Figures 3-4). The explanation for better intramuscular performance (C83) is mechanistically sound and supported by citations. The factors affecting filter consistency (C85-C86) are properly cited and lead logically to the methodological recommendation (C87).

results.result: Between-muscle differences in accuracy were observed, with vastii and gastrocnemii showing lower precision and agreement than TA. The authors speculate this may be due to greater variation in muscle-specific activation between baseline and test contractions caused by muscle redundancy in multi-joint movements. Decreased activation could cause peaks to be classified as noise, while increased activation could recruit spatially overlapping motor units causing merged sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 present an observed phenomenon (C91, supported by data in Figure 5) but the explanation is explicitly speculative (C92-C94). While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and supported by citations, no direct evidence is provided to test these hypotheses. The connection to experimental observations (C95) is inferential. This represents a reasonable interpretation but requires further investigation to confirm.

results.result: Sex-related differences in motor unit yield were observed, with females showing lower yields (9±12) than males (30±13), consistent with prior literature reporting approximately two-fold differences. The cause remains unclear but may relate to tissue properties, muscle fiber characteristics, or innervation ratios. Evidence for sex-related differences in motor unit properties comes primarily from animal studies, though recent simulation frameworks may help elucidate human differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 document an observed sex difference (C101) that is consistent with prior literature (C100). The acknowledgment of uncertainty about causation (C102) is appropriate. The speculation about possible mechanisms (C103) is reasonable but explicitly uncertain. The limitation that evidence comes from animal studies (C104) and the suggestion for future simulation work (C105) are appropriately cautious. The result is supported in documenting the observation and its consistency with literature, though mechanistic understanding is limited.

results.result: Manual editing of motor unit discharge times is essential for improving accuracy and is highly reliable across operators. The silhouette value (SIL) measures normalized distance between spikes and noise after k-means classification. Manual editing after blind-source separation shows high inter-operator reliability, with median agreement of 99.6% across 126 motor units and 8 operators with varying experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38, C88-C90 establish the importance and reliability of manual editing. The necessity of manual editing (C36, C88) is supported by multiple citations and demonstrated in the study's own data (Figure 2). The high inter-operator reliability (C89-C90) is supported by citation to prior work, providing confidence in the subjective aspects of the method. The SIL metric definition (C38) is properly cited.

results.result: To address challenges with varying activation levels, the authors propose updating motor unit filters and centroids during resting periods rather than continuously (which is computationally demanding). They recommend operators display motor unit pulse trains between contractions to check decomposition accuracy throughout sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 present proposed solutions to identified problems. While dynamic updating is supported by citations as a potential solution (C96), its computational demands are also documented (C97). The authors' proposal to update during rest periods (C98) and recommendation for between-contraction monitoring (C99) are reasonable suggestions but represent untested proposals rather than validated results. These are methodological recommendations for future implementation.

results.result: The real-time processing pipeline uses 125 ms epochs (256 points at 2048 Hz for surface, 1280 points at 10,240 Hz for intramuscular). Peaks are detected with minimum 25 ms separation. Firing rate is calculated as spike sum over 8 consecutive 125 ms epochs (1 second window), introducing 500 ms delay but facilitating participant control based on pilot testing. Additional smoothing uses a 4-value (500 ms) moving average.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 describe technical implementation details that are internally consistent and clearly specified. The trade-off between delay and controllability (C114) is explicitly acknowledged and justified by pilot testing. The parameter choices (epoch duration, window sizes, minimum peak separation) are clearly documented, enabling reproducibility. These are straightforward methodological descriptions.

results.result: Motor units transduce neural signals into force, with each motor neuron action potential eliciting action potentials in all innervated muscle fibers. Real-time decoding of motor neuron firing activity can enhance understanding of movement control and is essential for interfacing with external devices. Applications include virtual hand control by individuals with spinal cord injury and learning to independently control motor units within the same muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These are well-established principles in motor control (C1-C3) and documented applications from prior work (C4-C7). All claims are properly attributed to prior literature and represent accurate characterization of the field rather than novel findings of this study.

results.result: Traditional motor unit identification uses needle/fine-wire electrodes to identify few motor units during weak contractions. Recent electrode array developments enable larger recording zones and multi-channel recording. Blind-source separation algorithms can decode many motor units by optimizing separation vectors that maximize pulse train sparseness. Current open-source implementations are offline only. Recent studies report real-time capabilities using a two-step approach (offline training, real-time application), but no publicly available algorithms exist and systematic testing across muscles/intensities is lacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 provide literature review and gap identification. The characterization of traditional methods (C8), recent developments (C9-C11), and current limitations (C12, C14-C15) are all supported by appropriate citations. The description of the two-step approach (C13) accurately represents prior work. These claims establish the context and rationale for the current study.

results.result: During stationary conditions, motor unit action potential trains can be modeled as convolution of delta functions (discharge times) and consistent action potential shapes. Action potential shapes differ across electrodes due to varying conduction velocities and fiber locations relative to electrodes. Increasing electrode number and density increases likelihood of unique motor unit action potential profiles, which is necessary for accurate blind-source separation. Motor units with similar profiles will be merged by the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 describe the signal processing model and theoretical basis for the approach. The convolution model (C20) is standard in EMG signal processing. The explanation for spatial variation (C21) is based on established biophysics. The relationship between electrode density and discriminability (C22) is supported by citations. The necessity of uniqueness (C23) and consequence of similarity (C24) follow logically from the blind-source separation approach.

results.result: The software is recommended for use during stationary conditions (isometric contractions) to maintain motor unit filter consistency. The main purpose is to display real-time visual feedback based on individual or population motor unit activity. The smoothing filter duration is user-configurable. The authors hope the software will enable neuroscientists to design experimental paradigms studying neural control at the motor neuron level.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C106, C108-C109 describe intended use and capabilities. The recommendation for isometric contractions (C33) is supported by citations and follows from the algorithm requirements discussed elsewhere. The statement of purpose (C106) is straightforward. The configurability (C108) is a software feature. The hope for future applications (C109) is appropriately framed as aspirational rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Twenty-nine individuals (4 females, 25 males; 28±5 years; 178±6 cm; 73±16 kg) participated. None reported lower limb injury or pain in the prior 6 months. Ethical approval was obtained from appropriate committees and all participants provided informed written consent.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 provide standard participant demographics and ethical compliance information. The information is clearly stated and includes appropriate details. Ethical approval numbers are provided (C129). These are straightforward methodological details required for human subjects research.

results.result: The authors developed an open-source software package for real-time motor unit decomposition from EMG signals using blind-source separation (fastICA). The software was validated on data from five lower limb muscles using surface and intramuscular electrode arrays, with both synthetic and experimental validation approaches.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the value and validity of the software package. Reviewer 1 states the 'validation of the software package is compelling, suggesting that it can be successfully applied across a range of muscles and tasks.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the clarity of the presentation' and that 'Figures are especially effective.' Reviewer 3, after revision, confirms 'the method will be of use to the field.'

results.result: Manual editing of automatically decomposed motor units improved silhouette (SIL) values from ~0.82-0.89 to ~0.89-0.91 across muscles at 20% MVC, with a significant number of motor units removed during visual inspection. A SIL threshold of ~0.9 can be used to automatically filter poor quality motor unit pulse trains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about manual editing and quality metrics. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'statistical analyses are excellent,' which would encompass these quantitative results. The methodology for quality assessment and manual editing is accepted without critique.

results.result: Validation using synthetic EMG signals showed offline decomposition achieved near-perfect accuracy (99.2-100% rate of agreement). Real-time decomposition maintained high accuracy when applied to signals at the same force level (96.3-98.4%) or lower force (99.5-99.8%), but accuracy decreased when applied to higher force levels (80.3-88.6%) due to recruitment of spatially overlapping motor units.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'Validation of the software package is compelling, suggesting that it can be successfully applied across a range of muscles and tasks.' The simulation results demonstrating force-dependent accuracy are not questioned by any reviewer, indicating acceptance of these validation findings.

results.result: Experimental validation in tibialis anterior showed real-time decomposition achieved 93.9-95.6% rate of agreement when test and baseline forces matched. Accuracy decreased when filters were applied across different force levels (83.3-87.9%), with decreased sensitivity when applying higher-force filters to lower forces and decreased precision when applying lower-force filters to higher forces, confirming that newly recruited motor units disrupt decomposition accuracy.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 affirms the validation is 'compelling' across 'a range of muscles and tasks.' No reviewer challenges the experimental validation results or the interpretation that force level changes affect accuracy. The findings are treated as methodologically sound.

results.result: Testing across multiple muscles (VL, VM, GL, GM, TA) at 20% and 40% MVC showed variable accuracy, with highest rates of agreement for TA (93.6-97.3%) and lower rates for vastii (75.3-84.0%) and gastrocnemii (81.0-88.1%). The number of identified motor units ranged from 10-94 depending on muscle and electrode type.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes the validation demonstrates the software 'can be successfully applied across a range of muscles and tasks.' The between-muscle differences in accuracy are presented as findings without reviewer challenge, indicating acceptance of these results as valid characterization of the method's performance.

results.result: The RMSE between real-time and edited firing rates was consistently below 2 pulses per second across all muscles, with lowest values for TA (0.44-0.64 pps). These low RMSE values demonstrate that the visual biofeedback accurately represents motor unit firing activity to participants.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'statistical analyses are excellent,' which encompasses these RMSE findings. No reviewer questions the accuracy of the biofeedback or the interpretation that low RMSE indicates accurate representation of firing activity. The results are accepted as demonstrating the software's capability for real-time feedback.

results.result: Computational time analysis showed spike identification averaged 4.9±3.0 ms for surface electrodes (0.37 ms per motor unit) and 32.0 ms for intramuscular arrays (due to higher sampling frequency). Total computational time including visual feedback display was always shorter than the 125 ms epoch duration, making the system truly real-time.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'the key advance presented here is that the software provides real time identification' and praises the 'clarity of the presentation.' The computational performance data supporting real-time capability is not challenged by any reviewer, indicating acceptance of these technical specifications.

results.result: Lower accuracy in vastii and gastrocnemii compared to TA may be due to greater variability in muscle-specific activation between baseline and test contractions caused by muscle redundancy. Changes in activation level can cause peaks to be misclassified as noise (decreased activation) or result in merged sources from newly recruited spatially-close motor units (increased activation).
results.evaluation: While this is presented as speculation by the authors, no reviewer challenges this interpretation of the between-muscle differences. The explanation is consistent with the accepted experimental findings and is treated as a reasonable interpretation of the observed variability.

results.result: Motor unit yield from surface EMG was substantially lower in females (9±12) than males (30±13), consistent with prior literature. The cause remains unclear but may relate to tissue properties, muscle fiber properties, or innervation ratios, though evidence for sex differences comes primarily from animal studies.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges the reported sex differences in motor unit yield or questions the authors' acknowledgment of uncertainty about underlying mechanisms. The finding is presented as an important consideration for implementation, and reviewers accept this characterization without critique.

results.result: The blind-source separation algorithm requires uniqueness of motor unit action potential distributions across electrodes and consistency of motor unit filters over time. Intramuscular arrays provide higher accuracy than surface electrodes due to lower likelihood of spatially overlapping potentials. The approach is recommended for isometric contractions with stable force to maintain filter consistency, and manual editing is necessary and highly reliable across operators (99.6% agreement).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these methodological requirements and limitations. Reviewer 1 notes the validation is 'compelling' and Reviewer 2 praises the 'clarity of the presentation,' suggesting the explanation of algorithm assumptions and requirements is well-accepted. The necessity of manual editing and its reliability are not questioned.

results.result: To overcome challenges with varying activation levels, the authors propose updating motor unit filters and classification centroids during resting periods rather than continuously (which would be computationally demanding). They recommend operators display pulse trains between contractions to monitor decomposition accuracy.
results.evaluation: While these are proposed solutions rather than tested results, no reviewer challenges these recommendations. Reviewer 3's comment that 'the method will be of use to the field' after revision suggests acceptance of the authors' approach to addressing limitations, including these proposed solutions.

results.result: The software's main purpose is to provide real-time visual feedback based on individual or population motor unit activity. The smoothing filter duration is user-adjustable, and the authors hope the open-source software will enable neuroscientists to design new experimental paradigms for studying neural control at the motor neuron level.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the great potential that real-time decoding will provide' and Reviewer 3 notes after revision that 'the method will be of use to the field.' These statements affirm the software's intended purpose and potential impact as described by the authors.
